60/40 portfolio.long:
Sixty per cent equities, forty per cent bonds, rebalanced periodically. It is the default balanced allocation in most of the industry, and it functions less as a strategy than as the benchmark everything else has to beat before it deserves attention.

The reasoning is straightforward. Equities carry the growth and most of the volatility; bonds pay a coupon and have historically risen when equities fell, because the conditions that hurt company earnings — recession, falling demand — are the conditions in which central banks cut rates and bond prices rise. That negative correlation is the entire mechanism, and it does the work that makes the mix smoother than either leg alone.

Rebalancing is not an afterthought. Selling whatever grew to buy whatever shrank is what mechanically enforces selling high and buying low, without requiring any forecast at all.

Where people get fooled: treating the negative correlation as a law. It is a tendency that depends on inflation being contained — when inflation is the thing driving markets, both legs fall together, because rising rates hurt bonds directly and equity valuations at the same time. 2022 demonstrated that plainly. A diversifier that fails precisely in the conditions you most needed it is a real risk, not a footnote, and it is the assumption worth checking before leaning on this mix.
60/40 portfolio.usage: Generally the reference allocation an active strategy must beat after costs; its bond leg cushions equity falls only while inflation stays contained.

Permanent portfolio.long:
Harry Browne and Terry Coxon's design splits capital evenly across four assets — stocks, long bonds, gold and cash — and rebalances back to equal weights when they drift far enough apart. It was set out in Inflation-Proofing Your Investments in 1981.

The logic is regime assignment rather than forecasting. Each asset is chosen because it is expected to do well in one of four economic conditions: stocks in prosperity, long bonds in deflation, gold in inflation, cash in recession and tight money. The claim is not that all four rise together — it is that whatever the environment turns out to be, something in the portfolio is working, and rebalancing harvests from it.

That produces a deliberately unexciting result. It gives up a good deal of the upside a concentrated equity position would have captured, in exchange for far shallower drawdowns and much less dependence on being right about conditions.

Where people get fooled: expecting it to keep pace with equities during a long bull market, then abandoning it partway through for something that has been performing better. That is the failure mode of every defensive allocation — it is judged against the wrong benchmark in the good years and only looks sensible in the bad ones, by which point the person who switched is no longer holding it.
Permanent portfolio.usage: Typically held as a low-maintenance defensive allocation, rebalanced on drift bands rather than on a view about conditions.

All Weather portfolio.long:
Ray Dalio's All Weather allocates by risk rather than by capital. Instead of deciding what fraction of your money each asset gets, you decide what fraction of the portfolio's volatility each asset contributes, and size positions to equalise those contributions.

The consequence is counterintuitive. Bonds are far less volatile than equities, so equalising risk means holding much more of them by value — a risk-balanced portfolio can be seventy per cent or more bonds and still carry no more bond risk than equity risk. Institutional implementations then apply leverage to the bond leg so the whole portfolio reaches a target return without concentrating its risk in equities.

The framework is organised around four environments formed by growth and inflation each coming in above or below expectations, with assets assigned to the quadrant they historically suit.

Where people get fooled: the leverage is not optional decoration, it is structural, and retail versions that skip it are a different portfolio with a familiar name. Risk parity also depends on the volatility and correlation estimates staying stable, and both shift exactly when markets are stressed — the moment when a leveraged bond position is least forgiving. Judge it on drawdown and consistency, which is what it is built for, not on return.
All Weather portfolio.usage: Generally used as a risk-balanced allocation across growth and inflation regimes; the institutional version leverages the low-volatility legs.

Value averaging.long:
Michael Edleson's rule, from a 1988 article and the book that followed, sets a target path for what the portfolio should be worth at each date and invests whatever is required to hit it. If markets fell, you contribute more than planned; if they rose, you contribute less, and in a strong enough rise you sell the excess.

It is the disciplined extension of dollar cost averaging. Fixed contributions already buy more units when prices are low, but passively; value averaging enforces it, scaling the purchase to the size of the shortfall. Over a volatile path that produces a lower average cost per unit than fixed contributions do.

The cost is that contributions become unpredictable. A sustained decline demands progressively larger payments precisely when income is least secure and confidence is lowest, which is the same tension every buy-the-dip rule creates, made explicit and mandatory.

Where people get fooled: backtests assume the contributions were always made. The rule only delivers its advantage if you can and do fund the largest demands, and those arrive in exactly the months people cut back. A version with a cap on the maximum contribution is a different rule with different results — test the one you would actually follow, not the one on the page.
Value averaging.usage: Typically used for accumulation on a schedule, contributing the shortfall against a target value path rather than a fixed sum.

Dogs of the Dow.long:
At the start of each year, buy the ten Dow components with the highest dividend yields, hold them for twelve months, then re-rank and repeat. Michael O'Higgins popularised it in Beating the Dow in 1991.

The mechanism it leans on is real enough to name. Within a set of large, established companies, a high dividend yield usually means the price has fallen rather than the dividend has risen, so the screen mechanically selects the least-loved members of an index of survivors. That is a value tilt applied to a universe that has already been filtered for size and durability, which limits how badly wrong any one holding can go.

Its virtues are that it is completely mechanical, rebalances once a year so costs stay trivial, and requires no judgement about any company.

Where people get fooled: the record that sold the book was a backtest, run over a period the author selected, and published after that period had happened. The Dow's own membership is also decided by a committee that removes struggling companies — so the universe is survivorship-filtered by construction, and a strategy that buys the weakest members of a curated list of winners is quietly relying on that curation. Results since publication have been far less striking than the ones that made it famous.
Dogs of the Dow.usage: Generally run as an annual mechanical value screen on a large-cap index; its universe is curated by committee, which is part of the result.

London breakout.long:
Mark the high and low of the quiet Asian session, then trade the break of that range as London opens and participation steps up. It is one of the most widely taught FX session plays.

Unlike most named setups, the mechanism here is structural rather than assumed. FX liquidity genuinely follows the working day, and the London open is the largest single step up in participation in the twenty-four-hour cycle. A range built during thin hours is a range built by few participants, so it is easy to leave once the volume arrives. That much is plumbing, not folklore.

What the setup does not supply is direction or persistence. A range with a lot of volume arriving can break either way, and the same surge that carries a genuine breakout also produces the sharpest false ones — which is why the counter-trade, fading the failed break back into the range, is taught just as widely.

Where people get fooled: every parameter is a choice, and the choices are usually inherited rather than tested. Which hours count as the Asian session, how far past the edge counts as a break, whether a close is required, and how long after the open the setup expires — change any of them and you have a different strategy. From Perth, the London open lands mid-afternoon, which at least puts it in workable hours.
London breakout.usage: Typically traded on the majors at the London open, using the Asian range as the reference; the range and break definitions are parameters, not givens.

Wolfe wave.long:
Bill Wolfe's formation marks five turning points. A line drawn through the first and fourth projects forward to a target the fifth point is expected to travel to, giving both an entry area and a destination in one construction.

What distinguishes it from most pattern material is that it names a specific target rather than leaving the exit to judgement. That is genuinely more testable than a pattern with no stated objective — you can say in advance where the projection sits and record whether price got there.

The difficulty is upstream of that. Which swings count as the five points is decided by eye, and while a move develops the candidate points can be relabelled. Because the projection line is drawn through two of those points, moving a label moves the target, so the thing being tested is defined partly by what has already happened.

Where people get fooled: the precision of the projected line reads as rigour, but a precise consequence of an unfixed premise is not precise. The honest test is to fix the swing definition mechanically, mark the five points without hindsight, publish the target before the fifth leg, and count the misses — which is exactly the discipline that separates a testable rule from a shape people can always find afterwards.
Wolfe wave.usage: Generally traded as a reversal at the fifth point toward a projected line; the point-labelling is discretionary, so the target moves with it.

Three-drive pattern.long:
Three successive pushes in the same direction, each separated by a retracement, with the drives expected to hold specified proportions to one another. The third completion is read as exhaustion and traded against.

The observation underneath is ordinary and reasonable: extended moves often come in a few legs, and a third push arriving with less force than the first two describes a trend running out of participants. That is a fair description of momentum fading, and it does not require any of the ratio machinery layered on top.

The machinery is where it becomes fragile. Requiring each drive to hold a particular proportion sounds strict, but the requirement is applied with a tolerance, and the tolerance is rarely stated. A wide band finds the pattern constantly; a narrow one finds it almost never. Neither version has published validation.

Where people get fooled: symmetry is something the eye supplies. Three pushes that look evenly proportioned in review were three pushes of assorted sizes while they were forming, and the retrospective chart flatters the pattern enormously. Fix the tolerance and the swing definition before judging it, then count every occurrence including the ones where the third drive simply kept going — which, in a strong trend, is most of them.
Three-drive pattern.usage: Typically traded as exhaustion at the third push; the proportion requirement needs a stated tolerance before it means anything.
